items.stem: To add a new integration to Synnduit, what do you do?

options.text: Modify the Synnduit engine's source code
Implement a source connector (feed) and a destination connector (sink); the engine diffs them
Write a SQL script that copies data between databases

items.explanation: You supply the two connectors; the fixed engine computes and applies the delta. The engine binary is never edited.

misconceptions.a: The engine is fixed — you extend it via connectors and override points, not by editing it.
misconceptions.c: Hand-written copy scripts lose the mappings, change history, and delta detection the engine provides.
misconceptions.d: The destination schema is owned by the destination system, not something you change to add an integration.

items.stem: Put the pieces of the Synnduit data flow in order, from where data originates to where it lands.
items.explanation: Source → engine → destination. The engine sits in the middle and applies only the delta to the destination.

items.stem: Which part of the work does the Synnduit engine handle for you (rather than you writing it)?

options.text: Reading the raw data out of the source system
Comparing the new snapshot to last run and applying only the changes (the delta)
Knowing the source system's specific API or query language
Knowing how to create/update records in the destination system

items.explanation: Diffing the snapshot and applying the delta (plus mappings, change history, dedup, thresholds) is the engine's job. Reading the source and writing the destination are your connectors.

misconceptions.a: Reading the source is the feed's job — yours.
misconceptions.c: The source-specific access is exactly what your feed provides.
misconceptions.d: Destination create/update/delete is the sink's job — yours.

items.stem: A colleague says "Synnduit does as much as possible out-of-the-box but treats developers as first-class citizens." In terms of the engine model, what is fixed and what is yours to write?
rubric: Fixed/engine: the diffing/delta + bookkeeping (mappings, change history, dedup, thresholds, GC) — written once, not edited by you
Yours: the source connector (feed) and destination connector (sink), i.e. the system-specific code; default behavior can be overridden
items.sampleAnswer: The engine — delta detection, mappings, dedup, change logging, thresholds, garbage collection — is fixed and reused. You write the system-specific connectors (the feed that reads the source, the sink that writes the destination), and you can override default behaviors where needed.

items.stem: Why does CSSD report roughly a 75% reduction in custom code by using Synnduit?

options.text: The hard, reusable parts (diffing, dedup, change logging, thresholds, GC) live in the engine, so teams only write system-specific connectors
Synnduit generates the destination's user interface automatically
It eliminates the need for any source-side code

items.explanation: The engine absorbs the mechanically hard, error-prone logic once; per-integration work shrinks to writing connectors, cutting custom code dramatically.

misconceptions.d: You still write source-side feeds — but far less plumbing than a hand-rolled sync.
